4077.dq: One final vowel process is vowel reduction to a [ə] which can occur in word initial, unstressed, open syllables as represented in (16). (16) vowel ---> ə in an open, unstressed, word initial CV syllable
4077.dloc: §3.1 Syllable and Word Structure, print p. 6; §3.3.2 Vowel Variations and Processes, rule (16)-(17), print p. 12; §3.5.1 Tone Inventory and Description, print pp. 13-14; §4.3 Tone Inventory and Variations, print p. 18; §2 print p. 5 for the second-hand Morse 1960 remark.
4077.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Lacid is described as a tone language: three contrastive tones (high-fall, high-mid, low) in open/nasal-final syllables, two (high, low) in checked syllables, plus a stiff/slack voice-quality contrast. The only stress content is that the word-initial CV syllable of (mostly bisyllabic) words can be unstressed, in which case its vowel reduces to [ə] (reduced presyllable Cə) and it loses contrastive tone, taking its pitch from the following syllable; i.e. the sesquisyllabic minor-syllable pattern, prominence implicitly on the final (major) syllable. No positional stress rule computable from syllable count is given.
4077.srule: Not mentioned in Wannemacher 2011 (§3.1 p. 6, §3.3.2 p. 12, §3.5 Suprasegmental Inventory and Processes pp. 13-15, §4.3-4.4 p. 18, §5 p. 19 read): the suprasegmentals described are tone and voice quality only.

4077.tone: Wannemacher 2011: three phonemic tones (high-fall 54/53/52/51/41, high-mid 35/45/43/4/3, low 31/32/3/2/21) in unchecked syllables, two (high, low) in checked syllables; all tones occur with both stiff and slack voice; tone sandhi and possible register conditioning by initial consonant noted; 'Reduced syllables do not carry contrastive tone' and the reduced initial syllable assimilates its pitch to the following syllable. Stress appears only as the adjective 'unstressed' for the word-initial reduced CV syllable; no stress contrast, no stress rule, no phonetic correlates of stress described. Second-hand (Morse 1960 orthography ms., reported p. 5): on /ʔ/-final syllables 'Words with stress have a high tone... Unstressed words have a low tone', which Wannemacher does not adopt. Luk 2017 p. 16: three pitch tones (high, mid, low) plus creaky voice, 'a reduced presyllable Cə'; the words stress/accent/prominence do not occur in that thesis (full-text search). Kachin-portal sketch (Sawada): 'Lacid is a tone language', four tones, nothing on stress.

4078.heavy: Not stated in Lau-specific words. The Lau rule is identified with 'the general principle of measure-penultimate stress (Schütz 1976)' [p. 161], a mora-counting principle in which a long vowel is two vowels. The source's own long-vowel conventions are pan-Fijian: 'Underlying long vowels are marked with a macron. They are realized as long vowels on the surface except when preceding an unstressed vowel. For example SF (Standard Fijian) dōnu-∅... is realized as dōnui with the transitive suffix -i, but as donu when intransitive: *dōnu is not an acceptable form.' [p. 4]; 'penultimate long vowels are not allowed in Fijian' [p. 15 n. 3, citing Scott 1948:743]; 'a position in which long vowels are disallowed by a phonotactic constraint common to all Fijian languages' [p. 154]; 'disallowing a long vowel before an unstressed syllable' [p. 156]. What measure-penultimate stress does with a long vowel is stated by Schütz himself (1985, in the copy consulted, OA p. 613): 'it occurs on any long vowel or diphthong; in measures without long syllables, it occurs on the penultimate vowel'. Heavy = long vowel (CVV); Fijian syllables are open, so codas play no role; in Lau ai/au are two syllables, not diphthongs [p. 30], so they are not heavy, unlike Standard Fijian.

4079.prule: No word-stress rule is stated for Lutuv. Lutuv is described as a tonal language with three surface pitches (H, L, M; rise/fall across a bimoraic syllable), the tone analysis being 'in its infancy'. Words are major syllables (CV or CVŋ, bimoraic) optionally preceded by a minor syllable (Cə, monomoraic, 'very short'), the pair forming a 'sesquisyllabic' CəCV structure that the authors label 'iambic'. The only use of the word 'stress' by the Lutuv fieldworkers is a family-level definition in Lotven et al. 2020 (JSALL, aop p. 15, sec. 5), made for Proto-Kuki-Chin and 'nearly all modern Kuki-Chin languages': 'In sesquisyllabic words, a stressed "major syllable" is preceded by a short, unstressed C or CV "minor syllable" (also called a reduced, pre-, or semi-syllable), resulting in an iambic (unstressed-stressed) word structure.' That is a template statement (reduced non-final minor syllable vs full major syllable), hedged to the family, and not asserted for Lutuv; no Lutuv-specific source (the IWPSALC squibs, the Swadesh list, Lotven 2020, Lotven 2021 sec. 2.7, Lotven 2023) states a stress rule.

4080.prule: Stress falls on the mainsyllable, which is the final (and, in >98% of the lexicon, the only) syllable of the phonological word; a minorsyllable, when present (21 lexical items with a phonemic minorsyllable, plus partial reduplications), precedes it unstressed. Fixed-final, quantity-insensitive, position given by word shape. COMPOSITE/INFERRED: Jacq 2001 never formulates a stress rule; its only stress token is 'unstressed', said of the reduplicative minorsyllable vowel (p. 130; the concessive 'while unstressed' presupposes unstressedness as the normal property of minorsyllable vowels, but the phonemic minorsyllable vowel is itself described only as 'phonetically extra short in length', p. 117). The explicit 'stressed mainsyllable' statement is the co-authored family-level sentence, Sidwell & Jacq 2003: 33, for West Bahnaric languages generally; Jacq 2004: 98 ties it to Jru' ('a typical West Bahnaric language in respect to its word structure and phonemic inventory').

4093.prule: Fixed penultimate stress, quantity-insensitive (Balese has no phonemic vowel length; the length of the penultimate syllable is the exponent of the stress), stated in one clause for the word, the word complex and the syntactic unit: Vorbichler 1967 p. 452, under the heading 'Tone and stress', 'In Balese a long syllable, not being virtually disyllabic, always indicates a stress on the penultimate of a word, word complex, or syntactic unit.' In the 1965 grammar the same prominence is called Drucklängung (stress-lengthening) and assigned to the penultimate vowel of every morpheme, compound, syntagm and sentence, the sentence's own penult being the strongest. Balese is at the same time a tone language with three distinctive tonemes (high, low, and a mid that Harries treats as a slipped high), tone lexical in nominals and grammatical in verbals.
4093.srule: Within the simple word, none: Vorbichler 1965 §4 enumerates one Drucklängung per word, on its penult (họcà, iberi, merini). Lesser graded prominences only in compounds and phrases: each member of a compound keeps a Drucklängung on its own penult (ugba-héhí: /u/ and /é/) and each word or syntagm in a sentence keeps its penultimate Drucklängung, the sentence penult being the strongest (§4, §237). Not mentioned in Vorbichler 1967 p. 452.

4095.heavy: Not a stress rule, but the only weight remark: a long (CVV) first syllable of a disyllabic word is 'heavy' in comparison to the following syllable and 'attracts stress' (Watters 2002:40); CV first syllables give 'equal weight... and stress'. Vowel length is contrastive only in open syllables (Vesalainen 2016:5: 'For vowels /i, a, u, o/ the length is contrastive in open syllables, if we ignore the pitch contours (melody). Length never occurs in closed syllables, but it does occur in the second syllable, though more rarely'); Vesalainen fn. 1 adds that he does not claim length 'is contrastive by iself' since 'the pitch contours (rising and falling melodies) are somehow connected to the vowel length'.
4095.dflt: None stated; with a short first syllable 'the first and second syllables seem to be of equal “weight” in terms of quantity and “stress”' (Watters 2002:40).
4095.prule: No word-stress rule. Lhomi words belong to a high or a low register (clear/tense vs breathy-creaky/lax phonation; Vesalainen argues vowel quality, not pitch, is contrastive; Watters treats it as a two-register 'syllable tone' language whose syllable pitches derive from onset phonation and rhyme weight). Stress is mentioned only as a correlate: high-register words are 'more stressed' than low-register ones, and in disyllables a long (contrastively lengthened) first syllable 'attracts stress' or is lengthened because stressed; both remarks are explicitly hedged as unconfirmed.

4095.tone: Two-register system. Vesalainen 2016:6: 'A Lhomi word is either a high register word or a low register word' (clear vs breathy phonation); 'the pitch is not very well audible with most male speakers'; 'I argue that it is the vowel quality (tense/lax) that is contrastive, not the pitch'; the first syllable determines the pitch and voice quality of the whole word (fn. 2: 'If he means that it is the first syllable that determines the pitch and voice quality of the whole word, I fully agree'). Watters 2002:43: the rising/level pitch of long first syllables is 'due in part, I suggest, to the stress given to the first syllable. In low register, the influence of stress manifests itself as a rising pitch. In high register, stress induces a level pitch'; 'moon' vs 'monkey' are 'contrastive in analogous environments for pitch and stress' and not predictable from onset phonation. Watters 2002:44 (sec. 6.3 Summary): Lhomi is a 'syllable tone' language in which 'the pitch of a syllable is derived from its segmental characteristics, both from the quality of the onset and the weight of the rhyme'; 'These syllable pitches, however, are not phonologically contrastive'. Stress is thus a phonetic correlate of register and first-syllable length, never a contrastive or positional system.

tn.quote: A Lhomi word is either a high register word or a low register word. This means that the phonation of the vowels is either clear or breathy. This is the salient feature of Lhomi tonology. ... My observation is that the pitch is not very well audible with most male speakers. It is the clear and creaky vowels that help the hearer to distinguish between high and low register words. ... I argue that it is the vowel quality (tense/lax) that is contrastive, not the pitch. High register (tense) words are also more stressed than the low register ones (word stress).

4096.tone: Section 6 (p. 192): 'There are four lexical tone contrasting as high, mid, low and extra low in Liangmai and this has been observed in all varieties of Liangmai that I have studied so far.' Earlier studies (Amos 2007; Mataina & Pandey 2009; Pandey 2014: 413; Charengna 2011, 2017; Raguibou 2015; Daimai G. 2016; Daimai K. 2021) reported three levels; Mataina 2014: 71 and this paper give four. p. 193: the syllable is the TBU; prefixes of sesquisyllables seem to carry inherent tone (tsə̏ká 'friend' vs tsə̏lȕ 'field'); verbal-suffix tone is often influenced by the root; phrasal tone alternation exists. 4098.tone: Three level tones (high, mid, low), five word-level patterns (H, M, L throughout; HL; MHL), some words HL -> HM (marked in the Totota orthography, item d). Stress is described as 'automatic', non-distinctive and derived from tone: first H-toned syllable, else initial syllable; correlates loudness and slight length. The Welmers 1962: 86 statement (second-hand via the Stanford Phonology Archive digest in the copy consulted) agrees: non-phonemic, tone-conditioned, with the first high or low tone of the word, never with mid tone. The two differ only for words with no high tone and a mid tone before any low: the handbook puts stress on the first syllable, Welmers (per SPA) on the first low tone and never on mid; for all-mid words the handbook (p. 190) gives initial stress while the Welmers digest gives no stress.
